newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe students march against fees, corruption.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe students march against fees, corruption.

text.p: Thousands of Zimbabwean university students demonstrated in central Harare on Wednesday against the introduction of fees and alleged corruption in President Robert Mugabe's government.
From 3,000 to 4,000 University of Zimbabwe students marched into the city centre, singing, dancing, shouting obscenities and distributing statements denouncing the government.

Hundreds of riot police warily watched the protest, which police said they allowed after assurances it would be peaceful. Two weeks ago, police used teargas to stop the students from marching into the city centre during a class boycott.

Mugabe's cash-strapped government introduced a 50 percent fee at state-funded universities and colleges, but the students -- who used to get a 100 percent government grant -- say the move is unfair and will deny the poor higher education.
"The reason the government cannot afford our fees is because it is wasteful and corrupt," a student leader charged in an address outside parliament, repeating an accusation the government denies.
He was wildly cheered as he attacked Mugabe, already under severe public criticism, for allegedly condoning rising corruption in his administration and in the southern African state in general.

In a petition to parliament, the students alleged there was gross mismanagement and corruption in the way government tenders were awarded, saying they were only going to relatives of Mugabe and his wife, some close political associates and his tribesmen.
"Beneficiaries of multi-billion dollar public tenders sadly seem to emerge either from the ruling province in this country or from the two ruling families owing to coincidence or design," it said.

"There is need for government policies to retain a national and not tribal outlook," it said, adding some of the political and business elite were also abusing a programme, aimed at empowering Zimbabwe's black majority, to enrich themselves and their cronies.

Mugabe denies the government tender board is favouring his relatives and in particular his nephew Leo Mugabe, who has recently won three multi-billion dollar contracts in a row, sparking unprecedented controversy.
